symbols.name: AntigravityAdapter
symbols.note: Adapter for Google/Antigravity 'agy' over SSH. Disabled by default; requires signed_in=True. Uses ssh to run agy -p - with prompt on stdin.

symbols.name: AntigravityAdapter.__init__
symbols.note: Initializes adapter with ssh_target, effort, signed_in, ssh_command, runner, and sets endpoint.

symbols.name: AntigravityAdapter.argv
symbols.note: Returns list of command-line arguments for ssh and agy.

symbols.name: AntigravityAdapter._dispatch
symbols.note: Executes the model via SSH, parses response, returns status dict.

symbols.name: OllamaAdapter
symbols.note: Adapter for Ollama over /api/chat contract. Only class docstring and beginning shown; no methods in this chunk.

claims.text: The prompt goes on STDIN (``agy -p -``) and NEVER on a command line.
claims.why: Code in argv() includes '-p' and '-' as separate arguments, and _dispatch passes stdin_text=text to runner, so prompt is on stdin.

claims.text: ``ssh`` with a trailing command does not take an argv: it concatenates its arguments and hands the string to the REMOTE login shell, which re-parses it.
claims.why: This is a factual statement about SSH behavior; code uses subprocess list form which avoids local shell but remote shell will concatenate the list into a string and parse it. The code is consistent with this risk.

claims.text: The prompt here is a diff written by a candidate model, so an ordinary patch containing backticks or ``$(...)`` -- a shell script, a test log, a Python f-string -- would execute on the bench as Administrator, with no adversarial model required.
claims.why: The code passes the prompt via stdin_text to the runner, which will be sent over SSH. The remote shell will interpret the text, so shell injection is possible. The code does not sanitize the prompt.

claims.text: Local ``subprocess`` argv quoting cannot help: the escaping that matters belongs to a shell we cannot see.
claims.why: The code uses list form for subprocess, which quotes arguments for the local shell, but the remote shell will re-parse the concatenated string. The claim is accurate.

claims.text: ``agy`` has not completed its one-time interactive sign-in on this machine, so this adapter is DISABLED BY DEFAULT: it reports ``unavailable`` / ``not_authenticated`` immediately rather than hanging on an auth prompt.
claims.why: In __init__, signed_in defaults to False. In _dispatch, if not self.signed_in, it returns status 'unavailable' with reason 'not_authenticated' immediately.

claims.text: An operator asserts sign-in with ``signed_in=True``; nothing here probes it, because probing means invoking a model.
claims.why: The code only checks the boolean flag; no authentication probe is performed.

claims.text: The host is passed EXPLICITLY per call. ``OLLAMA_HOST`` is never read for routing and never written -- see the module docstring; normalising a remote Ollama into this process would silently flip ``offload.py``'s trusted lane.
claims.why: No code for OllamaAdapter is present in this chunk beyond the docstring; the module docstring is not provided.
The class definition is cut off; no implementation of 'local' attribute or method is shown.

observations.what: AntigravityAdapter docstring warns about shell injection via remote shell, but code does not sanitize the prompt.
AntigravityAdapter._dispatch returns 'not_authenticated' when signed_in is False, consistent with docstring.
AntigravityAdapter.argv constructs ssh command with -T, BatchMode=yes, ConnectTimeout=5, StrictHostKeyChecking=yes, which are sensible for automation.
OllamaAdapter class docstring references module docstring and offload.py, but no code in this chunk to verify.
_auth_failure method is defined but not used in this chunk; possibly inherited or used elsewhere.
